newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Easterners to miss landmark EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Easterners to miss landmark EU summit.

text.p: The European Union has decided to break with custom and not invite candidates from eastern Europe to its next summit in Amsterdam, diplomats said on Monday.

The decision, taken during a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday, was taken to allow EU leaders to devote all their attention at the landmark summit on June 16-17 to finalising the fine print of revisions to the EU treaty.
"There is no hidden motive," said one diplomat, adding that the easterners would be invited to meet around a week later.
It has become a custom for the EU to invite candidate members to summits for a dinner discussion and to take part in the family photo.

The Amsterdam summit will fall at a particularly tense time for the easterners as they await the European Commission's advice to EU governments on who is adequately prepared to start membership talks and who is not.
The EU executive has undertaken to publish its individual advice on each country shortly after the EU treaty review -- intended to prepare the EU for the day it has up to 25 members -- is finalised.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have all applied for membership, but the EU has not yet decided whether to open immediate talks with all of them or just those it judges are ready to join.
Romania, generally seen as struggling to meet the EU criteria, urged the Union on Monday to open talks with all applicants at the same time.
The EU intends to open talks six months after it finishes the treaty review.

"We do hope that within six months all the candidate countries will be able to start the negotiations at the same moment," Romania's Foreign Affairs Minister Adrian Severin told a news conference after meeting EU foreign ministers.
He said that while talks should start at the same time for all countries, each one should be admitted as soon as it has met the criteria for membership.

Estonian foreign minister Toomas Hendrik Ilves, whose country is generally believed to have a good chance of joining the EU's first enlargement wave, said talks should open at once, but should then proceed on merit and nothing else.
"Pre-selection is something which can have very dangerous consequences," he told reporters after meeting EU and eastern European foreign ministers.

He said that by favouring certain countries because of their geopolitical situation, or in order to compensate them for being left out of the NATO military alliance's own first enlargement wave, the EU would be sending the wrong signals - discouraging those who have taken reforms seriously, encouraging those who have been lax to continue being so.
